blocks.text: PPO, proximal policy optimization, is the reinforcement learning algorithm classically used to actually update a model weights during RLHF, covered in the earlier RLHF topic, using the reward model score covered in the previous topic to guide small, carefully constrained updates rather than large, potentially destabilizing ones.
This topic explains what makes PPO specifically proximal, and why its complexity has motivated the simpler direct preference methods, DPO, ORPO, and KTO, covered elsewhere in this module.

PPO stands for proximal policy optimization, a reinforcement learning algorithm, and the word proximal is the key detail, covered directly later in this topic, describing how it specifically constrains updates to stay close to the model previous behavior.

Within the RLHF pipeline covered in the earlier topic, PPO is the specific algorithm responsible for taking the reward model score from the previous topic and translating it into an actual weight update, playing the same fundamental role an optimizer like AdamW, covered in the Optimizers module, plays for supervised fine-tuning, but adapted for a reinforcement learning setting.

In reinforcement learning terminology, the model being trained is called the policy, since it defines a strategy, or policy, for what action, in this case what token, to generate next given the current context, the same underlying next token prediction task covered throughout this course, just framed in reinforcement learning language.
4. Why "Proximal", Limiting How Far Updates Can Go

blocks.alt: Why "Proximal", Limiting How Far Updates Can Go

blocks.text: PPO specifically limits how much the policy can change in any single update step, preventing the kind of large, potentially destabilizing update that a naive reinforcement learning approach might otherwise make, staying proximal, close, to its previous behavior rather than swinging wildly based on a single reward signal.

A common technique within PPO adds a penalty term based on KL divergence, a measure of how different the updated model behavior is from its starting point, discouraging the model from drifting too far from its original, already fine-tuned behavior even while optimizing for the reward model score.

# A conceptual sketch of PPO's constrained update
new_policy_output = updated_model(prompt)
kl_penalty = measure_kl_divergence(new_policy_output, original_model_output)
total_loss = reward_signal - kl_penalty_weight * kl_penalty

blocks.text: A PPO training loop repeatedly generates responses using the current policy, scores those responses using the reward model covered in the previous topic, and applies a small, constrained update based on that score, cycling through this loop many times to gradually shift the model behavior toward higher reward responses.

blocks.title: This complexity is exactly what motivated the simpler alternatives covered elsewhere in this module
blocks.content: PPO requires maintaining and coordinating several moving pieces at once, the policy being trained, the reward model, and careful hyperparameter tuning for the KL penalty, a genuinely more involved setup than the more direct methods covered in the DPO, ORPO, and KTO topics.

blocks.text: PPO training involves several interacting components, the policy, the reward model, and the constrained update mechanism, all needing careful coordination and tuning, a genuinely more complex setup than the supervised fine-tuning covered throughout most of this course.

DPO, covered in an earlier topic, was specifically developed to achieve similar alignment goals as PPO based RLHF without needing a separate reward model or the full reinforcement learning loop, a meaningful simplification that has made it a popular alternative for many alignment training projects today.

blocks.text: Despite the rise of simpler alternatives, PPO based RLHF remains an actively used approach, particularly in settings where its specific reinforcement learning framing offers advantages over the more direct preference optimization methods, and understanding it clearly helps make sense of why those simpler alternatives were developed in the first place.

A team running a full RLHF pipeline uses PPO to update their model based on reward model scores, carefully tuning the KL divergence penalty to prevent the model from drifting too far from its original, already helpful fine-tuned behavior while still improving toward higher reward responses.

After several rounds of the generate, score, and update loop, their model shows measurable improvement in reward model scores while a spot check confirms it has not lost the core helpfulness established during its earlier supervised fine-tuning stage, exactly the balance the KL penalty was designed to help maintain.

items: Setting the KL divergence penalty too weak, allowing the model to drift too far and lose its original fine-tuned behavior
Setting the KL divergence penalty too strong, preventing the model from meaningfully improving toward the reward signal at all
Underestimating the complexity and coordination PPO requires compared to more direct preference optimization methods
Not validating the reward model quality, covered in the previous topic, before relying on it to guide PPO training

blocks.text: In your own words, explain why PPO includes a KL divergence penalty limiting how far the updated policy can drift from its starting point, rather than simply optimizing purely for the highest possible reward model score.

PPO is the reinforcement learning algorithm classically used within RLHF to update a model based on reward model feedback, specifically constraining each update to stay proximal to the model previous behavior through a KL divergence penalty, and while its complexity, coordinating a policy, a reward model, and careful tuning, has motivated simpler direct alternatives like DPO, it remains a foundational and still actively used technique in alignment training.
